reference.source: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A distinct demyelinating disorder recognised as separate from multiple sclerosis and from aquaporin-4-positive neuromyelitis optica
Common phenotypes include optic neuritis (often bilateral with marked disc swelling), transverse myelitis, and, in children particularly, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM)
Antibodies target myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein on the outer myelin surface, and patients are characteristically aquaporin-4 antibody negative
Attacks are frequently steroid-responsive but relapse on steroid withdrawal, so tapering must be cautious
Optic neuritis tends to show longitudinally extensive anterior optic nerve involvement with perineural enhancement
Antibody testing should use a live cell-based assay, and low-positive titres require cautious interpretation

Acute attacks are treated with high-dose corticosteroids, with intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange for severe or refractory episodes, and relapsing disease may need longer-term immunotherapy
reference.pathophysiology: The disorder is associated with immunoglobulin G antibodies against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG), a protein expressed on the outermost lamellae of central nervous system myelin and the oligodendrocyte surface. Antibody binding, together with complement and cellular effector mechanisms, produces inflammatory demyelination that preferentially affects the optic nerves, spinal cord, and, in children, the cerebral white matter and deep grey structures. In contrast to aquaporin-4 disease, astrocytes are relatively spared and demyelination can be more reversible, which correlates with the frequently good recovery from individual attacks.
additionalDifferentials: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Serum MOG-IgG by a live cell-based assay with attention to titre
Aquaporin-4 antibody testing to distinguish neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder
MRI of the brain, orbits, and spinal cord to characterise lesions and enhancement
Optical coherence tomography and visual evoked potentials for optic nerve involvement
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis, which shows oligoclonal bands less often than in multiple sclerosis
Screening for infective mimics before immunosuppression
redFlags: Severe or bilateral visual loss from optic neuritis
Longitudinally extensive myelitis with sphincter or respiratory compromise
Encephalopathy or seizures in an ADEM-like presentation
Frequent relapses on steroid tapering indicating need for maintenance therapy
reference.prognosis: Recovery from individual attacks is often good, but a relapsing course occurs in a substantial minority and repeated attacks can accumulate visual or spinal disability. Prognosis is generally more favourable than aquaporin-4 disease when relapses are prevented.
pitfalls: Misclassifying the disorder as multiple sclerosis and starting inappropriate disease-modifying drugs
Over-interpreting low-positive antibody titres, especially with an incompatible phenotype
Tapering corticosteroids too quickly and precipitating relapse
Assuming aquaporin-4 disease without confirming antibody status
